title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026]
Title:Self-Evolving Agent Harness
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at this https URL.

report.summary: A new 66-page paper formalizes "harness self-evolution": agents that rewrite their own prompts, memory, workflows and code while model weights stay frozen.
report.background: Since 2023, most agent capability gains have come not from retraining models but from scaffolding — the prompts, tool schemas, memory stores, retry logic and orchestration code wrapped around a frozen LLM. Projects like AutoGPT, SWE-agent and OpenHands showed that harness quality often matters more than the base model. But harness edits are usually hand-tuned by humans, and improvements are rarely preserved across runs or validated rigorously. This paper treats the harness itself as the learnable object: a feedback loop where proposed revisions are admitted or rejected using fresh validation data, then persisted. It sits at the intersection of evolutionary program search, continual learning theory, and agent safety, and frames harness recursive self-improvement (RSI) as an engineering discipline with testable guarantees rather than an ad-hoc prompt-tweaking practice.
key_points: Weights stay frozen, scaffolding changes. The paper defines harness self-evolution as editing prompts, memory, workflows, tool definitions and executable components while the underlying model is untouched — making "learning" a software-engineering and search problem rather than a training problem.

Revision is a governed pipeline, not a free-for-all. The framework explicitly separates what can be updated (interpreted state, code/tools, repository control logic, plugin composition) from how changes are proposed and how they are admitted, with accepted revisions persisting across future runs.

Theory supplies safety rails. Using evolutionary optimization for search and continual PAC-learning for reliability, the authors derive an expected generalization bound, a retention bound tied to a regression budget, and a high-probability admission rule requiring fresh, independent validation data.

Deployment demands ongoing validation. Because task distributions and evaluators drift, the paper argues reliable use requires continual re-validation plus separate safeguards for the learning loop, runtime privileges, and any consequential real-world actions.

Broader stakes are organizational. Persistent harness revisions affect how knowledge is shared inside teams, and the authors tie this to scientific reproducibility, physical safety and institutional accountability for autonomous systems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes agent improvement as a governed release process: harness changes become versioned artifacts with regression budgets and admission tests, much like CI/CD for prompts and tools. For developers, it implies new tooling — eval harnesses, rollback infrastructure, permission boundaries between the learning loop and runtime privileges — and could reduce the cost of agent maintenance while raising the bar for evaluation rigor. For regular users, agents may quietly get better at recurring tasks without model upgrades, but the paper's own emphasis on drift, regressions and accountability signals that persistent self-editing is also a risk surface: an agent that rewrites its own memory and workflows needs auditability, and enterprises will likely need to decide how much unsupervised self-modification they permit.
report.tools: To follow this line of work, watch DSPy (programmatic prompt/pipeline optimization), LangGraph and AutoGen (workflow and multi-agent orchestration), OpenHands and SWE-agent (open coding-agent harnesses), Letta/MemGPT (persistent agent memory), and AgentOps or LangSmith for tracing and evaluation. The paper's own GitHub repository, plus MCP for plugin/tool composition, are the most direct starting points for reproducing harness-evolution experiments.
